tldr: This paper proposes Variable Impedance Diffusion Policy (VIDP), which learns both required compliance and trajectory motions simultaneously without force sensors from kinesthetic demonstrations collected across diverse spatial layouts. By decoupling geometric variation caused by layout changes from intentional compliance, VIDP achieves high success rates and safety in contact-rich tasks where purely stiff or overly compliant controllers fail.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of VIDP. On the left, kinesthetic demonstrations are collected across diverse spatial layouts. On the top right, the proposed TP-DAMM extracts physically consistent, directionality-aware trajectory distributions. On the bottom right, target stiffness profiles are generated from these variances and fed into a Diffusion Policy, which jointly predicts end-effector poses and stiffness from images and proprioception to drive a variable impedance controller.
overview:
When robots perform contact-rich manipulation tasks such as parts assembly or cable routing, balancing tracking accuracy with mechanical compliance to absorb external forces is essential. Variable impedance control dynamically adapts stiffness across task phases, but tuning it manually for every scenario is extremely tedious. Imitation learning from human demonstrations offers a promising path, yet inferring required compliance from force-agnostic kinematic data (positions and velocities only) has remained an open challenge.

The core difficulty is that collecting demonstrations across varied spatial layouts introduces trajectory variations that confound geometric adaptation with intentional compliance. Existing statistical models (such as TP-GMM or DAMM) struggle to untangle differing reference frames from reversed motion directions, failing to extract appropriate stiffness profiles.

To overcome this, the authors introduce the Task-Parameterized Directionality-Aware Mixture Model (TP-DAMM). By modeling angular deviations of motion directions within local reference frames of task landmarks, TP-DAMM extracts true task degrees of freedom and variances from diverse demonstrations. Mapping the inverse of these variances to stiffness profiles, the authors build VIDP, a diffusion-based visuomotor policy that jointly predicts end-effector poses and stiffness directly from camera images.

Evaluated on three contact-rich real-robot tasks using a Franka arm (peg-in-hole, pulley assembly, and cable routing), VIDP significantly outperformed fixed-impedance baselines (always stiff or always compliant). It also reduced excessive contact forces, minimized tracking errors, and decreased mechanical energy consumption.
contributions: Proposed TP-DAMM to decouple geometric adaptation from intentional compliance across diverse demonstration layouts, extracting physically consistent trajectory distributions.

Constructed VIDP, an imitation learning framework that automatically maps trajectory variances to target stiffness and jointly predicts end-effector poses and stiffness from images and proprioception without force sensors.
Demonstrated on a physical Franka robot across three challenging contact-rich tasks that VIDP substantially outperforms fixed-impedance baselines while reducing contact forces and tracking errors.

sections.heading: Why does a robot need to adjust its stiffness dynamically?
sections.summary: Contact-rich manipulation demands both high tracking accuracy and safe compliance. However, learning suitable stiffness from force-agnostic kinematic demonstrations faces the fundamental obstacle of distinguishing layout-induced trajectory variations from intentional compliance.
sections.details:
When collaborative robots tackle precision assembly like peg-in-hole or handle flexible objects like cables, a static compliance setting falls short. For instance, inserting a peg into a tight hole requires yielding laterally to avoid jamming, while pulling a cable requires applying sufficient force without fighting its tension excessively. In other words, dynamic variable impedance control that modulates end-effector stiffness throughout task progression is indispensable.

Because analytically deriving impedance tuning rules from environmental models is difficult, imitation learning from human demonstrations has gained attention. However, a major problem arises: when demonstration data consists purely of kinematic trajectories (positions and velocities), target stiffness remains an unobservable hidden variable.

The situation becomes even more complicated when gathering diverse demonstrations to generalize across varied layouts and poses. Looking at trajectory variations, one cannot tell whether they stem from geometric adaptations to shifted layouts or intentional compliance to release contact forces.

Prior approaches sidestepped this issue by relying on force sensors or restricting demonstrations to identical starting configurations, incurring hardware dependencies or limiting generalization. To address this, the authors propose VIDP, which derives physically consistent stiffness profiles directly from positional demonstrations and jointly predicts actions and stiffness via diffusion models.

sections.heading: How to learn compliance without force sensors?
sections.summary: Many contact-rich manipulation methods rely on force-torque sensors or specialized teleoperation devices. However, sensor noise, synchronization overhead, and specialized hardware present practical barriers, making approaches that infer stiffness purely from kinematic data highly desirable.
sections.details:
Traditional hybrid position/force control and impedance control depend on manual parameter tuning and geometric environmental models, limiting adaptability in unstructured settings. Reinforcement learning (RL) has been used to learn stiffness policies, but trial-and-error exploration on hardware entails safety risks and prohibitive sample complexity.

Hence, learning compliance from human demonstrations has gained significant traction. While some methods fuse vision with real-time force-torque sensing, most off-the-shelf cobots do not come with high-precision force sensors, and synchronizing noisy high-frequency force data with lower-frequency camera feeds is difficult. Alternative techniques that require operators to manually toggle stiffness modes or use specialized tactile/AR equipment also increase the data-collection burden.

Conversely, statistically estimating stiffness from the inverse of trajectory variance across demonstrations (soft along high-variance directions, stiff along low-variance ones) has long been explored. However, conventional methods assumed a single fixed global frame, causing them to fail when task target locations shift across trials.

VIDP addresses these limitations by leveraging a task-parameterized, directionality-aware statistical model that extracts valid stiffness profiles from diverse kinematic demonstrations without any extra sensors.

sections.heading: Foundations of impedance control and limitations of task-parameterized models
sections.summary: This section reviews classical joint impedance control and Task-Parameterized Gaussian Mixture Models (TP-GMM) defined across local reference frames. Standard TP-GMMs fail when trajectories share spatial coordinates but move in opposite directions.
sections.details:
### III-A Classical Variable Impedance Control
With robot dynamics compensated, the commanded joint torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{cmd}$ is determined by a hybrid joint impedance control law.
Target stiffness $\mathbf{K}_{d}$ and damping $\mathbf{D}_{d}$ matrices in task space (end-effector frame) vary dynamically as the task progresses and are projected into joint space via the robot Jacobian $\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})$. To maintain contact stability, damping is coupled with stiffness via $\mathbf{D}_{d}=2\zeta\sqrt{\mathbf{K}_{d}}$, maintaining a constant damping ratio $\zeta$ (chosen as near-critical damping $\zeta=0.707$).

### III-B Task-Parameterized Probabilistic Representation
When task targets change locations across trials, observing trajectories relative to multiple candidate reference frames ($P$ task parameters) located at objects or the end-effector is effective. A global state $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}$ is locally transformed via translations $\mathbf{b}_{t,j}$ and rotations $\mathbf{A}_{t,j}$ for each frame $j$.

A well-known model is the Task-Parameterized Gaussian Mixture Model (TP-GMM). It learns Gaussian parameters in each local frame and, when faced with a new layout, projects them back into the global frame and fuses them using a Product of Gaussians (PoG). This produces a trajectory distribution satisfying geometric constraints across all frames simultaneously.

However, TP-GMM has a clear limitation. While it aligns spatial positions, it cannot distinguish trajectories that are spatially close but move in opposite directions (e.g., forward and backward passes), causing them to collapse into a single high-variance Gaussian. On the other hand, Directionality-Aware Mixture Models (DAMM) handle motion directions but operate only within a single frame, leaving them vulnerable to layout shifts.

sections.heading: Disentangling geometry from compliance and predicting both with a diffusion model
sections.summary: VIDP consists of three stages. First, TP-DAMM extracts direction-consistent trajectory distributions from diverse demonstrations. Next, trajectory variances are mapped to target stiffness profiles. Finally, a Diffusion Policy is trained to jointly predict end-effector poses and stiffness from vision and proprioception.
sections.details:
### IV-A Trajectory Distribution Estimation via TP-DAMM
To resolve the directional ambiguity of TP-GMM and the spatial rigidity of DAMM, the authors propose TP-DAMM.

- **Frame-wise Directional Augmentation**: Alongside end-effector position, the unit velocity vector $\boldsymbol{u}_{t}^{(j)}$ is incorporated. Based on Riemannian geometry on the unit sphere, angular deviations $d_{t,m}^{(j)}$ from each cluster's mean direction are computed via the logarithmic map. This cleanly separates demonstrations passing through the same spatial region in opposite directions into distinct clusters.
- **Probabilistic Formulation and Inference**: The covariance matrix is block-diagonalized assuming independence between spatial positions and directional variances, and likelihoods are evaluated using a Product of Gaussians across frames. Inference employs a parallel split-merge Gibbs sampler. By reducing dimensionality via PCA over concatenated local features, cluster splitting and merging remain stable even with small sample sizes.

### IV-B Mapping Distributions to Target Stiffness
Once clustering yields the integrated spatial covariance $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{m}$, an eigenvalue decomposition of the precision matrix (inverse covariance) is performed. Directions requiring tight tracking precision (low variance) receive large eigenvalues, while loose directions (high variance) receive smaller ones.
These statistical eigenvalues are scaled to the robot's allowable stiffness range $[\kappa_{\min}, \kappa_{\max}]$ to form the translational stiffness matrix $\mathbf{K}_{trans}^{m}$. A moving average filter is applied to smooth transitions between clusters and prevent control instability.

### IV-C Policy Learning and Real-Time Execution
Using the derived stiffness profiles as supervision labels, a visuomotor policy is trained.

- **Network Architecture**: A conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) is employed. RGB images from a wrist camera are encoded via a CLIP-pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT). The action output is a 15-dimensional chunk containing target position (3D), continuous rotation (6D), and the Cholesky factor (6 upper-triangular elements) of the stiffness matrix. Predicting Cholesky factors guarantees that reconstructed stiffness matrices remain symmetric and positive-definite.
- **Real-Time Execution**: Diffusion inference latencies can cause pauses or stuttering, producing hazardous contact force surges. To ensure smooth operation, the framework incorporates Real-Time Chunking (RTC) and optimal transport flow-matching guidance, preserving temporal consistency with previously executed plans while running asynchronously.

captions.F1: VIDP architecture overview. Diverse demonstration data is processed by TP-DAMM to estimate task-parameterized, direction-aware distributions. Variances are mapped into stiffness profiles, which a Diffusion Policy then uses to jointly predict end-effector poses and stiffness from images and proprioception.

sections.heading: Physical Franka evaluation: Automatic stiffness adaptation makes all the difference across three contact tasks
sections.summary: Evaluated on a physical Franka robot across peg-in-hole, pulley assembly, and cable routing tasks, VIDP achieved significantly higher success rates than fixed-stiffness baselines, while dramatically curbing excessive contact forces, tracking lags, and energy waste.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
Demonstrations were collected using a handheld UMI interface, a GoPro camera, and external motion capture, and evaluated on a Franka Emika robot. VIDP was benchmarked against two fixed-impedance diffusion baselines sharing identical architectures: Stiff-DP (1200 N/m across all axes) and Compliant-DP (400 N/m across all axes).
Three contact-rich tasks (20 physical trials each) were tested:
1. **Peg-in-Hole**: Rigid contact task involving approach, alignment, and insertion phases.
2. **Pulley Assembly**: Hybrid contact task requiring stretching an elastic band and seating it onto a groove.
3. **Cable Routing**: Deformable manipulation task requiring threading a flexible cable through three consecutive hooks.

### V-B Clustering Performance (TP-DAMM)
Evaluating clustering performance on real-robot datasets revealed that TP-DAMM achieved the lowest local and global directional variance and the highest cosine similarity compared to standard GMM, DAMM, and TP-GMM. Combining task frame alignment with directional awareness proved critical for accurately isolating true motion primitives.

### V-C Task Success Rates
- **Peg-in-Hole**: VIDP achieved an 80% success rate, matching Stiff-DP (80%), whereas Compliant-DP reached only 15% due to inadequate positioning accuracy. While Stiff-DP suffered jamming from excessive contact forces during insertion, VIDP dynamically lowered insertion-axis ($Z$-axis) stiffness while maintaining high lateral stiffness, enabling smooth insertions.
- **Pulley Assembly**: VIDP achieved a 70% success rate, nearly doubling Compliant-DP (40%) and Stiff-DP (35%). Stiff-DP lost the band due to excessive normal force causing slippage, and Compliant-DP lacked sufficient force to push it in. VIDP appropriately increased normal stiffness during stretching and raised lateral stiffness when seating the band.
- **Cable Routing**: VIDP reached a 75% success rate. Stiff-DP achieved 0% because it over-resisted cable tension and dragged the fixture, while Compliant-DP accumulated tracking errors due to excessive compliance, achieving only 60%. VIDP raised stiffness during hook entry for precision and reduced lateral stiffness during pulling to yield to tension.

### V-D Contact Forces, Tracking Errors, and Energy Efficiency
Detailed analysis of successful runs showed that Stiff-DP consistently produced large peak contact forces, risking hardware or workpiece damage. Compliant-DP succumbed to external loads, producing large tracking errors and repetitive hunting motions that inflated total energy consumption (absolute mechanical work). By staying stiff only when necessary and yielding elsewhere, VIDP achieved the best overall trade-off among contact forces, tracking errors, and energy expenditure.

captions.F3: Phase-wise analysis of successful and failed trials across the three tasks. The middle plot illustrates VIDP's predicted stiffness ($K_x, K_y, K_z$), dynamically adapting across task phases. The bottom plot shows how extreme contact force surges or tracking lags in fixed-impedance baselines (Stiff-DP and Compliant-DP) directly triggered task failures.

sections.heading: Conclusions and next steps: Tackling visual occlusions and intersecting trajectories
sections.summary: VIDP demonstrates that variable impedance skills can be acquired from diverse kinematic demonstrations without force sensors. Future work aims to automate task frame discovery and address visual occlusions where the end-effector hides contact points.
sections.details:
This work introduced VIDP, an imitation learning framework that acquires variable impedance manipulation skills purely from force-agnostic kinematic demonstrations. By decoupling spatial layout shifts from intentional compliance using TP-DAMM and predicting poses and stiffness jointly via a diffusion policy, the method achieves safe and robust execution across complex physical contact tasks.

Nonetheless, several limitations remain.
First, TP-DAMM requires candidate task reference frames (such as object or target positions) to be predefined by humans. Fully autonomous deployment will require mechanisms that discover these relevant frames directly from data.
Second, handling highly complex topologies where trajectories self-intersect remains challenging.
Third, when the robot's end-effector or the manipulated object occludes the contact zone from the camera, visual feedback responsiveness degrades. The authors plan to extend the framework to enhance reactivity under partial observability and model more intricate trajectory distributions.

takeaways: When inferring stiffness from demonstration variance, incorporating task reference frames alongside directional angular deviations (Riemannian log-map) cleanly separates layout-induced geometric variations from intentional compliance.
Predicting the Cholesky factor of the stiffness matrix within the action space of a Diffusion Policy guarantees positive-definite, symmetric stiffness tensors in an end-to-end visuomotor framework.

In contact-rich tasks, purely stiff controllers cause excessive forces and jamming, while overly compliant controllers induce tracking lag and wasteful oscillating motions; dynamic stiffness modulation across task phases is essential.
limitations: Candidate task reference frames (such as object poses or goal locations) used by TP-DAMM must be manually specified ahead of time.
Clustering highly complex motion patterns with self-intersecting trajectories in state space remains challenging.
Visual occlusions, where the end-effector or grasped object hides contact points, degrade the camera-based policy's ability to react promptly to changing contact dynamics.
